prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map separates the narrow grassy corridor from the two flanking structures: the siding wall is on the left, the brick wall is on the right, and the grass extends forward between them, while the dark upper regions generally indicate distant background or missing depth. Across frames 1–3, the dog moves from roughly 5–7 m ahead to about 2–3 m and then within approximately 0.5–1 m, becoming the nearest large object; in frame 3 it partly fills and occludes the lower-central view. Across frames 4–5, a person near the brick wall moves from roughly 3–4 m away to about 1–2 m, while distant cars remain approximately 8–15 m away beyond and to the right of that person. Brightness makes these approach relationships and the foreground-versus-background layout clearer than RGB alone, but the nearly uniform bright ground, haloed silhouettes, dark sky/background, and poorly resolved lower-edge objects make exact metric distances and fine occlusion boundaries unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates a dog in frames 1 and 3, a small person-shaped region in frame 2, a person in frames 4 and 5, and several cars in the far-right background, clarifying which separated image regions are distinct foreground instances. The dog shifts from left of center and roughly 5–7 m ahead to near center at about 2–3 m, then becomes a very large central mask within about 0.5–1 m; the frame-2 dog is also visible in RGB at center but appears to be mislabeled as a person, while a nearby sliver at the lower right is only partly in view. The later person remains ahead near the brick wall, changing from right of center at roughly 3–4 m to left of center at about 1–2 m as the camera turns or closes distance; the cars stay farther behind that person, mainly to the right, with some clipped by the image boundary. This map makes instance identity, overlap, and partial visibility easier to see than RGB alone, but it omits the walls and ground, gives no direct metric depth or facing direction, misses some visible regions, and contains evident class-label errors such as “perso,” “ccar,” and the frame-2 dog/person confusion.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects a small body skeleton in frame 2 and a much larger person skeleton with one magenta hand in frame 5, while frames 1, 3, and 4 contain no reliable pose despite visible animals or a person. In frame 2 the detected figure is near the horizontal center and several metres ahead, but the RGB indicates that this region is the approaching dog, so the human-shaped skeleton is unreliable and should not support a facing estimate. In frame 5 the person is about 1–2 m ahead and left of center; the torso and head are roughly frontal to the camera, the visible arm extends down toward the camera wearer’s side, and the magenta hand lies near the lower-left edge of the body, plausibly around arm’s-reach distance, while the other lower arm is less completely resolved. The skeleton exposes limb configuration and approximate body orientation more clearly than RGB alone, but missing detections, the false frame-2 pose, uncertain facial landmarks, and clipped or merged hand geometry prevent confident claims about gaze, exact distances, occluded limbs, or the separate camera-wearer hand visible at the bottom of the RGB frame.
